Subject: Dental Materials
Question: The term "trituration" means
Option B: Mixing of amalgam alloy and mercury
Explanation:
'B' [Phillips' 11th ed 523/ 12th ed 341]
Trituration is mixing of alloy and mercury. Usually, the alloy particles are coated with a film oxide, and this layer prevents the penetration of mercury. During trituration, the oxide layer is removed by abrasion so that a clean surface of alloy can come in contact with the mercury.

Spherical alloys usually require less amalgamation time than the lathe-cut alloys. Undertrituration results in weak restoration with rough surface. The rough surface will increase the susceptibility to tarnish.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Dynamic creep is the
Option A: Continuing alloying between silver-tin alloy and mercury during the life of restoration
Option B: Deformation of set amalgam during function
Option C: Process whereby alloy is "wetted" by mercury
Explanation:
'B' [Phillips' 11th ed 46, 540/ 12th ed 33,353]
Creep is the time dependent plastic deformation, which occurs when a metal is subjected to a constant load near its melting point. Restorations of higher-creep alloys generally experience greater marginal breakdown than the restorations with low-creep values.

Amalgams will undergo creep as its melting point is slightly above the room temperature. Dynamic creep is the deformation of set amalgam during function. The creep can cause an amalgam restoration, to extend out of the cavity preparation and increases its susceptibility to marginal breakdown.

The tin-mercury phase (γ₂) lacks corrosion resistance and is the weakest component of dental amalgam.

In high copper alloys, the gamma₂ (Sn₇Hg₈) is eliminated and replaced by eta (Cu₆Sn₅) phase, which is most resistant to tarnish and corrosion. As a result, the high copper amalgam alloys will have high strength, hardness and high corrosion resistance.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Discolourisation of Ag containing alloy is due to
Explanation:
'B & D' [According to key provided by the university; Check Explanation below]
Tarnish is an early indication and precursor of corrosion. In tarnish there will be surface discoloration or loss of lustre but no disintegration of the metals. Eg: Silver sulphide tarnish.

Two types of corrosion are:
• Chemical or dry
• Electrochemical or wet

Chemical (or) dry corrosion occurs in the absence of moisture. There is direct combination of metallic and non-metallic elements to form a chemical compound by oxidation, halogenation or sulfurization.

Eg: discoloration of silver by sulphur. So discoloration of silver containing alloys is both by tarnish and dry corrosion.

Wet corrosion requires presence of water or electrolyte as a pathway for the transport of electrons. It is more important for dental restorations. In oral cavity dry and wet corrosion cannot be distinguished separately due to the presence of saliva.

Question: Which of the following statements is not true about use of silica in the investment materials?
Option C: Quartz and cristobalite are the allotropic form used in dental investments
Option D: Beta allotropic form is stable below transition temperature
Explanation:
'D' [Check Q.No.9 and 64]
Silica exists in four alltropic forms
1) Quartz
2) Tridymite
3) Crystobalite
4) Fused quartz

When these allotropic forms are heated, a change in crystalline form occurs at a transition temperature characteristic of the particular form of Silica. Inversion temperature of Quartz (alpha) to quartz (beta) is 575°C; crystobalite (alpha) to crystobalite (beta) is 200-270°C and tridymite is 117-163°C. Beta allotropic form is stable only above transition temperature. Inversion back to lower alpha form occurs on cooling in each case.

No microstructural features can be mechanically separated into two or more phases, so only one solid phase is present.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Laser welding
Option B: Can be done with pure Titanium
Option D: Can be done with pure gold
Explanation:
'B' [Phillips 1st SA 418]

Laser welding in an argon gas atmosphere is a method of choice for joining titanium components of dental prostheses, because the coherent, high intensity laser pulse of light can be focused in a small region and melt the substrate without much damage to the surrounding areas. Also the joint will be composed of the same titanium, thereby preserving biocompatibility and avoiding galvanic corrosion.
